description: Calculate pressure altitude from pressure with the Pressure Altitude Calculator — the ISA formula pilots and altimeters live by. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, air pressure of 29.42 inHg at sea level corresponds to a pressure altitude of 467 feet — your altimeter, set to 29.92, would swear you are nearly 500 feet up while you stand on the ramp.
quick_answer: The Pressure Altitude Calculator converts an air pressure reading into pressure altitude — the height the International Standard Atmosphere assigns to that pressure. Enter the pressure and read the altitude in feet: the number aircraft performance charts, altimeter settings and density calculations all start from.
steps_intro: Pressure is altitude, spoken by the standard atmosphere:

body.t: Takeoff charts are indexed by pressure altitude (then corrected for temperature into density altitude). Compute the PA from the field's pressure before the chart work begins.

Watches and phones that report 'altitude' from pressure are doing this calculation with a sea-level reference you give them. Knowing the formula explains their weather-day drift.
Home stations report sea-level pressure by inverting this very relation with your elevation — set the elevation right, or every forecast model ingesting your data inherits the error.

Station pressure 28.50 inHg — a strong storm's figure — corresponds to a pressure altitude of about 1,340 ft at sea level. Aircraft on the ground 'believe' they are a quarter-mile up, and their takeoff performance genuinely worsens to match.

At 30.50 inHg, pressure altitude at sea level is about −531 ft — below the sea, in the standard atmosphere's bookkeeping. Negative pressure altitudes are legitimate outputs, and performance charts handle them fine.

popular_table.note: Pressure altitude is not true altitude — it is the standard atmosphere's interpretation of a pressure. Temperature then bends it into density altitude, which is what wings and engines actually feel.

faq: Density altitude is pressure altitude corrected for temperature — hot air thins, and the aircraft performs as if higher. PA is the first half of the calculation; every performance chart wants both halves done.

The standard atmosphere's sea-level pressure — the reference the whole system hangs from. Altimeters set to it read pressure altitude directly, which is why airliners above the transition altitude all fly on 29.92.
The same ISA relation in hectopascals: PA (ft) = 145,366.45 × (1 − (P/1013.25)^0.190284). One formula, two unit dialects — aviation outside the US mostly speaks hPa.
Why does my altimeter disagree with GPS altitude?
Because they measure different things: pressure (interpreted) versus satellite geometry. On non-standard days differences of 100–300 ft at altitude are unremarkable and expected.

The formula wants the actual pressure at the point (station pressure). Weather reports publish sea-level-reduced pressure (the altimeter setting) — feeding one as the other is the classic input error, worth roughly your elevation in feet of error.
